objections.objection: We don't have budget for another planning tool right now.
objections.response: Frame ketteQ as an overlay, not a rip-and-replace — it can run on top of the ERP/planning systems already in place (SAP, Oracle, Kinaxis, Blue Yonder, o9, Anaplan, Logility, or homegrown) and target the specific decisions costing the most in stockouts, excess inventory, or planner time today. Offer to model ROI on their own revenue and inventory numbers.

objections.objection: Our planners are managing fine with spreadsheets and our existing ERP today.
objections.response: Spreadsheet-based and ERP-native planning scale poorly as SKU count, channel complexity, and promotional activity grow. PolymatiQ automates the scenario work planners are doing manually today, and Salesforce-native commercial data means the plan reflects real pipeline, not just historical orders.

objections.objection: We're worried about trusting an AI-driven planning engine with real decisions.
objections.response: PolymatiQ's recommendations are transparent and auditable — planners review and approve, the system doesn't act unsupervised on high-stakes decisions. Propose a scoped pilot with a clear before/after metric (forecast accuracy, fill rate, planner cycle time) so trust is earned on their own data.

objections.objection: We're already committed to Kinaxis / o9 / Blue Yonder / SAP IBP / Anaplan / Logility.
objections.response: This usually isn't a replacement conversation. ketteQ can layer on top of that investment to accelerate specific decisions — especially ones that depend on Salesforce commercial data the incumbent doesn't natively see. See the relevant battlecard for the specific angle.

objections.objection: We're not on Salesforce for CRM — does ketteQ still make sense?
objections.response: The Salesforce-native UX is the differentiator, but the AWS-hosted PolymatiQ solver and planning data model integrate with SAP, Oracle, and homegrown systems regardless of CRM. Lead with the planning capability and integration roadmap rather than assuming Salesforce is a hard requirement.

objections.objection: How do you handle our ERP and commercial data securely?
objections.response: Walk through the Salesforce platform's enterprise security model plus AWS-hosted solver security posture. Contrast with the governance risk of planning decisions still happening in ungoverned, single-owner spreadsheets outside any system of record.

questions: How much planner time goes into manual scenario analysis or spreadsheet reconciliation every S&OP cycle?
Where do stockouts, excess inventory, or missed allocation opportunities rank among this year's priorities?
What's prompting you to look at supply chain planning software now versus 12 months ago?
What ERP and planning systems are in place today, and how well do they talk to each other?
Does sales pipeline or CRM data factor into the demand plan today, or is that a separate, manual step?
How do you measure forecast accuracy and S&OP cycle time today?
Who owns this decision on the supply chain / planning side, and who owns it on IT / finance?
What would a successful pilot need to prove for you to expand it enterprise-wide?
What's your timeline, and which budget cycle would this fall into?
Are you currently running or evaluating Kinaxis, o9, Blue Yonder, SAP IBP, Anaplan, or Logility?
What would make you choose an overlay/augmentation approach versus a full platform replacement?
